heading: Rivers, bison and country food
intro: Indigenous peoples in Treaty 6, across Alberta and across Inuit Nunangat hold detailed knowledge of the water, plants and animals that ecosystems depend on. That knowledge sits alongside the science of this lab: water cycles, matter cycles and food webs. These connections use Indigenous names for places, peoples and animals where a source gives them, and each name's source is listed at the bottom of its card.

connections.title: kisiskâciwani-sîpiy: the river that feeds amiskwacîwâskahikan
connections.text: The river that supplies Edmonton's drinking water has Indigenous names. The Canadian Heritage Rivers System writes them as kisiskâciwani-sîpiy and Omaka-ty. The City of Edmonton says the river's English name comes from the Cree word kis-is-ska-tche-wan, meaning "swift current," and that Omaka-ty is Blackfoot for Big River. The river remains a place for ceremony, gathering of medicines and subsistence. Former Chief Jerome Morin of Enoch Cree Nation says: "We've always had an affinity to the rivers, to the lakes, for transportation, for fishing, hunting trapping." The Cree called this area Amiskwaciy, Beaver Hills, and the fort amiskwacîwâskahikan, Beaver Hills House. Look for amisk, the beaver, in this lab's food web.

connections.title: Iinii and paskwâwi-mostoswak: buffalo return to Banff
connections.text: In 2017, Parks Canada moved 16 plains bison from Elk Island National Park to Banff. By 2024 the herd had grown past 130. In Blackfoot, buffalo is Iinii. In a Cree story, buffalo are paskwâwi-mostoswak. Parks Canada credits much of the project's success to weaving Indigenous ceremonies and cultural knowledge with western science. Partners include the Iyarhe Nakoda (Stoney Nakoda Nations), Siksika, Piikani, Kainai and Tsúut'ínà Nations, Samson Cree Nation and the Rocky View Métis District of the Otipemisiwak Métis Government. Bison are a keystone species: their grazing and wallowing create habitat, and moving herds spread nutrients. In the 2014 Buffalo Treaty, signing nations say buffalo "has been our relative."

connections.title: Iqaluk, Tuktu and Natsiq: country food and Arctic food webs
connections.text: For more than four thousand years, Inuit have lived on the land, marine waters and islands of the Arctic. ITK calls Inuit Nunangat the homeland of Canadian Inuit, and says country foods are central to Inuit culture and way of life. ITK's Arctic wildlife guide calls Iqaluk (Arctic char) "a favourite food of our people," says Tuktu (caribou) is one of the most important food sources for Inuit in Canada, and says Elders call seal a "special food." It records food web links: in northern Labrador, Qilalugaq (beluga) feed on Arctic char, and Nanuq (polar bear) hunt Natsiq (ringed seal) as their main food.

sources.title: Source of the names Iqaluk (Arctic char), Tuktu (caribou), Natsiq (ringed seal), Qilalugaq (beluga) and Nanuq (polar bear): Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami: Arctic Wildlife

Source of the names Iqaluk (Arctic char), Tuktu (caribou), Natsiq (ringed seal), Qilalugaq (beluga) and Nanuq (polar bear), same spellings: Canadian Geographic, Indigenous Peoples Atlas of Canada: Wildlife
Source of the name Inuit Nunangat (the homeland of Canadian Inuit): Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami: Inuit Nunangat Food Security Strategy

try: Parks Canada says plains bison were nearly extinct over 140 years ago, and that one result was reduced biodiversity. Use what you learned about food webs to predict what changes when Iinii, the buffalo, return to a grassy meadow. Which living things might increase, and why?

Parks Canada says moving bison herds spread nutrients through the ecosystem. Draw a matter cycle that shows how carbon and nutrients in grass could end up back in the soil after a buffalo eats it. Where do decomposers fit? Where might amisk, the beaver, fit in a food web along kisiskâciwani-sîpiy?

ITK's wildlife guide notes that in northern Labrador Qilalugaq (beluga) eat Iqaluk (Arctic char), and that Nanuq (polar bear) hunt Natsiq (ringed seal) as their main food. Build two short Arctic food chains from these links. Name the trophic level of each animal, and explain why there are far fewer polar bears than seals.

review_flags: How this revision applies your note ("Use the indigenous names whenever possible, and cite the source of each name"): Indigenous names now appear in the titles, peoples fields, texts, try prompts and slide points, and every name has a source in its card's Source line whose title begins "Source of the name(s) ...:". Names used and their sources: kisiskâciwani-sîpiy and Omaka-ty (Canadian Heritage Rivers System); kis-is-ska-tche-wan (swift current), Omaka-ty (Big River), Amiskwaciy (Beaver Hills), amiskwacîwâskahikan (Beaver Hills House) (City of Edmonton Archives); amisk, beaver (Dictionary of Canadianisms, UBC); nêhiyawak (Indigenous Saskatchewan Encyclopedia, USask); Niitsitapi (Real People), Iinii (buffalo), Siksika, Piikani, Kainai (Many Leaders) (Glenbow Museum, Niitsitapiisini); Siksika, Piikani, Kainai, Otipemisiwak Métis Government as partner names (Parks Canada); paskwâwi-mostoswak, buffalo (Cree Literacy Network); Iyarhe Nakoda ("peoples of the mountains"), Bearspaw, Chiniki, Goodstoney (Stoney Nakoda Nations); Tsúut'ínà (Tsuut'ina Nation); Otipemisiwak (the people who own themselves) (Otipemisiwak Métis Government); Iqaluk (Arctic char), Tuktu (caribou), Natsiq (ringed seal), Qilalugaq (beluga), Nanuq (polar bear) (ITK Arctic Wildlife, confirmed by the Indigenous Peoples Atlas of Canada); Inuit Nunangat (ITK Food Security Strategy). Question: the names are cited in each card's Source line. Would you also like a single "Names and their sources" list at the bottom of the Ways of knowing panel? That would need a small change to _build/iwk.py, which I can propose for your approval.

Spellings where sources differ, and names I could not source: (1) Blackfoot buffalo: Glenbow's Niitsitapiisini page writes Iinii (used); Glenbow's teacher toolkit glossary writes Iinnii (singular) and Iniiksii (plural); the Galt Museum writes Ii nii. (2) Cree buffalo: I found no source that glosses a Cree word as "plains bison," so I did not use paskwâwi-mostos. I used paskwâwi-mostoswak, which the Cree Literacy Network translates as "buffalo" (plural; its note also writes pâskwawi-mostosak). The Narwhal (Cree by Dorothy Thunder, University of Alberta) writes paskwâwimostos and paskwâw mostoswak; a 2015 book title writes paskwāwi-mostos. A Cree language speaker or itwêwina should confirm the preferred form; itwêwina and the Lethbridge Polytechnic iinii page were blocked for me this session. (3) Edmonton: the City writes amiskwacîwâskahikan; the Edmonton Public Library's Voices of the Land writes amiskwaciwâskahikan. (4) Stoney Nakoda: the Nations' own site writes Iyarhe Nakoda without circumflexes, so I did not use Îyârhe. (5) Blackfoot nation names: the Blackfoot Confederacy Tribal Council writes Siksikawa, Kainaiwa and Aapatohipiikunniwa; Glenbow writes Siksika, Kainai, Piikani (used). (6) Glenbow says Niitsitapi refers to "ourselves and all other First Nations people," so it is a little broader than "Blackfoot." (7) I found no sourced Stoney Nakoda word for buffalo or beaver, and no meaning for Tsúut'ínà on the nation's page, so none is given.

Fact correction from re-checking ITK's Arctic Wildlife guide: it says beluga feed on Arctic char in northern Labrador bays and fiords, not everywhere, so the text and try prompt now say "in northern Labrador." I also removed the earlier ITK Food Security line about wildlife management and harvesting to fit the names within 110 words; it is still true on that page if you want it back.

The Banff bison partner list comes from Parks Canada, not from the nations themselves. Parks Canada also lists the Ktunaxa and Shuswap Bands, which I left out to keep to Alberta nations; say if you want them added. Would you like me to look for each nation's own statement, or a Knowledge Keeper's published words, before this goes to students? I did not describe the ceremonies Parks Canada mentions, on purpose.

The ITK Arctic Wildlife document is older: its nutrition fact sheets are dated March 1996, though ITK still hosts it, and the Indigenous Peoples Atlas of Canada repeats its animal names. Is an older ITK source acceptable, or should I keep looking for a current ITK or regional Inuit source (for example Qikiqtani Inuit Association) on country food?

EPCOR is a utility, not an Indigenous-led source. I used it only for Former Chief Jerome Morin's own quoted words from EPCOR's video series. Acceptable, or prefer to drop it? Similarly, the Cree Literacy Network and the Dictionary of Canadianisms are not nation-run; a Cree-led dictionary entry would be a stronger source for amisk and paskwâwi-mostoswak.

Existing lab content (Lesson on the water cycle, and the runoff diagram): the note that Edmonton's drinking water comes from the North Saskatchewan and flows east through Treaty 6 territory still has no citation in the lab. The Canadian Heritage Rivers System page says the river "played a key part in the signing, oral history, and shared understanding of Treaty No. 6." Should I add that page as the note's source, and should the lab's note also use the name kisiskâciwani-sîpiy?

I left out a Peace-Athabasca Delta or peatland carbon connection to keep to three well-sourced scales. If you want the carbon cycle covered directly, I can research an Indigenous-led peatland or wetland stewardship example next.

Overlap across labs: the Banff bison project and the Buffalo Treaty also appear in the drafts for Biodiversity and Stability and Disturbance and Succession. Keep it in both labs as a thread students can follow, or should I replace this one with a different connection? If kept, those drafts should get the same names and Source lines so the labs match.
